summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and prior right hallux amputation for gas gangrene was admitted due to new erythema and yellow drainage around his surgical wound. He was evaluated for possible recurrent infection but found to have no fever, leukocytosis, or radiographic signs of osteomyelitis or soft tissue gas. The changes were attributed to benign healing changes and increased granulation tissue. Podiatry performed a bedside debridement and determined no acute surgical or infectious intervention was needed. The patient remained stable, continued on oral augmentin, and was discharged home the following day with instructions to follow up for wound grafting and monitor for signs of infection.
problems: Amputation of limb(s) causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
